title: EEOC's H-1B Bias Warning Fuels Anti-Indian Backlash
excerpt: A federal hiring-bias crackdown targeting H-1B preferences is being seized upon by anti-immigration activists to stoke hostility toward Indian tech workers.
body:
EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas put U.S. employers on notice in November 2025, releasing a technical assistance document titled 'Discrimination Against American Workers Is Against the Law' — and anti-H-1B activists wasted no time turning the federal warning into fresh ammunition against Indian tech workers.

**What the EEOC actually said:**
On November 19, 2025, the EEOC released a one-page fact sheet warning that job postings stating 'H-1B preferred' or 'H-1B only' violate Title VII of the Civil Rights Act. The agency also flagged disparate treatment in firing, compensation, and promotions as unlawful. Chair Lucas declared that 'unlawful bias against American workers is a large-scale problem in multiple industries nationwide.' The Department of Labor amplified the message five days later, crediting the guidance to its own cross-agency enforcement drive, *Project Firewall*.

**How activists are twisting it:**
The EEOC guidance targets employer misconduct — not immigrant workers themselves. Yet online communities hostile to high-skilled immigration immediately reframed it as official validation of their claims that Indian H-1B holders are displacing American workers. An Indian tech manager in the U.S. described in November 2025 a sharp rise in workplace hostility and online rhetoric, with colleagues reading enforcement investigations as proof that 'hiring was already skewed in favor of H-1B workers.' According to USCIS data, Indians hold 71 percent of all H-1B visas — making the community the most visible target of this backlash. The AAPI Equity Alliance separately documented a surge in anti-South Asian slurs across social media platforms tied directly to H-1B debate.

**What to watch:**
With Project Firewall coordinating the EEOC, DOJ, and DOL into a unified enforcement front, employers will face rising scrutiny through 2026 — and Indian-American professionals will need to watch whether that pressure translates into measurable hiring discrimination against them on the ground.
